newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's euro promoter resigns after 3-wk stint.
newsitem.headline: Austria's euro promoter resigns after 3-wk stint.

text.p: A campaign by the Austrian government to prepare the country for Europe's single currency suffered a setback on Thursday when its chief promoter resigned amid allegations he towed the EU commission's line.

Gustav Raab, former head of the Association of Austrian Savings Banks, threw in the towel after barely three weeks on the job, widely considered a key part of the government's strategy to boost flagging support for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
"I can confirm that he has put in his resignation," a spokeswoman for Raab's office at the Austrian finance ministry told Reuters.

Raab had come under a barrage of criticism for being under contract with the European Commission to hold speeches on the euro if and when called upon by the European Union's executive body. According to the agreement, he would have been obliged to promote the EU's official line on the single currency.
Raab told Austrian state television earlier this week he had never actually been asked by the Commission to hold such a speech.

In a letter faxed to Austrian news agency APA on Thursday, Raab said he had resigned from his EU commission duties before taking up his promotion job for the Austrian government but that he feared he had lost so much public confidence that he could no longer fulfil his task properly.
"The government's representative has to exude trust so that people accept the euro. I am not a liar," he said.
"An objective and trustworthy information of the population is so important that it should not be tainted by a discussion about myself," Raab added.

The opposition Greens, among Raab's fiercest critics, earlier on Thursday accused him of having turned the government's information campaign into a "propaganda act" and called for a new concept in line with "the most primitive ground rules of democracy".

A spokesman for Austrian finance minister Rudolf Edlinger said he had just received the news of Raab's resignation and was unable to comment on it, but added a successor was likely to be chosen over the next few days.
According to recent polls, a mere 15 percent of Austrians believe the introduction of the Euro will benefit them, while some 50 percent fear for the value of their savings.
